learn.hook: Who is the real winner — the one who comes first, or the one who never gives up?
points: 'The Winner' is a poem about what it really means to win: effort, courage and not giving up.
A poem can make us rethink a word. Here, 'winning' means doing your best, not only coming first.
Couplets are pairs of lines that rhyme. A poem made of rhyming couplets has the rhyme scheme AABBCC...
Poets use images like 'a fire inside' to show strong feelings such as determination.
Read a poem aloud to feel its rhythm — the beat of strong and soft sounds.

example.q: Read this original poem: I tripped on the track and I heard the loud cheer / For the runners ahead as the finish drew near; / My knees were all scraped and my laces untied, / But I stood up again with a fire inside. / I came in last, but I crossed the line — / And the medal of trying is shining and mine. Why does the speaker feel like a winner?
steps: The speaker tripped, got hurt and came in last.
But they stood up again 'with a fire inside' and crossed the line.
They call their effort 'the medal of trying'.
example.answer: Because they did not give up — they got up and finished the race, and that effort is their 'medal'.

learn.reallife: School sports days give medals to the top three, but everyone who finishes the race has shown courage.

games.title: About the poem
items: The speaker came first in the race.
The speaker says, 'I came in last.'
The speaker tripped on the track.
The speaker gave up after falling.
The speaker stood up again and crossed the line.
It is an image for a strong will to keep going.
The poem is made of rhyming couplets.
Each pair of lines rhymes: cheer/near, untied/inside, line/mine.

quiz.q: In the poem, what happened to the speaker on the track?
options: The speaker won a gold medal
The speaker lost a shoe in the river
quiz.explain: Line 1: 'I tripped on the track.'
steps: Read the first line of the poem.
Line 1 says: 'I tripped on the track.'
So the speaker tripped and fell.
Answer: The speaker tripped and fell
quiz.mistake: Does not read the first line carefully

quiz.q: In the poem, the cheer was for:
quiz.explain: The cheer was 'for the runners ahead as the finish drew near'.
steps: The poem says the cheer was 'for the runners ahead as the finish drew near'.
The speaker had fallen behind.
So the cheer was for the runners ahead.
Answer: the runners ahead
quiz.mistake: Assumes the cheer was for the speaker

quiz.q: "But I stood up again with a fire inside." What does 'a fire inside' mean?
options: a real fire in the stadium
a strong determination to keep going
quiz.explain: It is an image showing a burning wish to finish.
steps: 'A fire inside' is an image, not a real fire.
It shows a strong, burning wish to keep going.
So it means a strong determination.
Answer: a strong determination to keep going
quiz.mistake: Takes the image literally

quiz.q: In the poem, in what position did the speaker finish?
quiz.explain: Line 5: 'I came in last, but I crossed the line.'
steps: Line 5 says: 'I came in last, but I crossed the line.'
So the speaker finished in the last position.
But the speaker still finished the race.
Answer: last
quiz.mistake: Assumes the 'winner' must have come first

quiz.q: What is 'the medal of trying' in the poem?
options: a medal bought from a shop
a medal for the fastest runner
the pride of having done one's best
quiz.explain: It is not a real medal; it stands for the reward of effort.
steps: 'The medal of trying' is not a real medal.
It stands for the pride of having done one's best.
The speaker earns it by finishing despite falling.
Answer: the pride of having done one's best
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally

quiz.q: What is the main message of the poem?
options: Not giving up makes you a winner
quiz.explain: The speaker finishes last but feels like a winner because of their effort.
steps: The speaker fell, got up and finished last.
Yet the speaker feels like a winner because of the effort.
So the message is that not giving up makes you a winner.
Answer: Not giving up makes you a winner
quiz.mistake: Thinks winning only means coming first

quiz.q: Two rhyming lines together are called a:
quiz.explain: A couplet is a pair of rhyming lines.
steps: A pair of rhyming lines together has a special name.
It is called a couplet.
'Paragraph' and 'chapter' are prose words.
Answer: couplet
quiz.mistake: Uses a prose word for a poem part

quiz.q: Which pair of words rhymes in the poem?
quiz.explain: 'Line' and 'mine' share the '-ine' sound.
steps: Rhyming words share the same ending sound.
'Line' and 'mine' both end in '-ine'.
Track/cheer, knees/laces and last/crossed do not rhyme.
Answer: line, mine
quiz.mistake: Picks words that are near each other but don't rhyme

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'The poem says the person who came last is a winner. How is that possible?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Winning means trying your best and never giving up — even if you come last. I'm a winner too!
teach.nudge: What did the speaker do after falling that makes them a winner?

revise.summary: 'The Winner' is a poem about what it really means to win: effort, courage and not giving up. Here, 'winning' means doing your best, not only coming first.
focus: Finding details from the poem's lines
Explaining images like 'a fire inside' and 'the medal of trying'
remember: Couplets are pairs of lines that rhyme; rhyming couplets have the rhyme scheme AABBCC...
Images like 'a fire inside' show strong feelings such as determination.
Rhythm is the beat of strong and soft sounds.
traps: Don't think winning only means coming first; the speaker came last but feels like a winner.
Don't take 'the medal of trying' literally; it is the pride of having done one's best.
The cheer was for the runners ahead, not for the speaker.

learn.hook: A spider fails seven times to climb its thread and climbs on the eighth. That spider knows a big word: perseverance!
points: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult or takes a long time.
Word family: persevere (verb), perseverance (noun), persevering (adjective). Similar words: determination, persistence, grit.
The opposite of persevering is giving up or quitting.
Proverbs about perseverance: 'Practice makes perfect', 'Slow and steady wins the race', 'Where there's a will, there's a way'.
Perseverance works best with good habits: setting small goals, practising daily and learning from mistakes.

example.q: Think it through: Neha cannot ride her bicycle and falls three times. She asks her brother to hold the seat and practises every evening for a week. Finally she rides alone. Which proverb fits?
steps: Neha keeps trying after falling.
She practises every day.
Her practice leads to success.
example.answer: 'Practice makes perfect' (or 'Where there's a will, there's a way').

learn.reallife: Learning to swim, playing a musical instrument or solving tough maths sums all need perseverance.

games.title: Proverb and meaning
pairs: doing something often makes you good at it
Slow and steady wins the race
Where there's a will, there's a way
if you really want something, you'll find a way
Rome was not built in a day

items.text: Her ___ helped her climb the hill.
He showed great ___ to finish the project.

quiz.q: What does 'perseverance' mean?
options: continuing to try even when it is hard
quiz.explain: Perseverance is steady effort in spite of difficulty.
steps: Perseverance is about effort.
It means continuing to try even when it is hard.
It is not luck or speed.
Answer: continuing to try even when it is hard
quiz.mistake: Confuses perseverance with luck or speed

quiz.q: Which is the opposite of 'persevere'?
quiz.explain: To persevere is to keep going; to give up is to stop trying.
steps: To persevere is to keep going.
The opposite is to stop trying.
So the opposite is 'give up'.
Answer: give up
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym

quiz.q: Which proverb means 'big things take time'?
options: Rome was not built in a day
Two heads are better than one
quiz.explain: It means great achievements need time and patience.
steps: We need a proverb about big things needing time.
'Rome was not built in a day' means great things take time and patience.
'Practice makes perfect' is about practice, not time.
Answer: Rome was not built in a day
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of the proverb

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'perseverance'?
quiz.explain: Persistence means continuing firmly — just like perseverance.
steps: A synonym has the same meaning.
Persistence means continuing firmly, like perseverance.
Laziness, impatience and carelessness are opposites.
Answer: persistence
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym

quiz.q: Which action shows perseverance?
options: Practising the tabla every day even when it is hard
quiz.explain: Daily practice through difficulty is perseverance.
steps: Perseverance means steady effort despite difficulty.
Practising the tabla every day even when it is hard shows this.
Stopping, breaking or passing it on show the opposite.
Answer: Practising the tabla every day even when it is hard
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise steady effort

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'determined'?
quiz.explain: 'Determination' is the noun; 'determine' is the verb.
steps: 'Determine' is the verb; 'determined' is the adjective.
The noun is 'determination'.
'Determinedly' is an adverb.
Answer: determination
quiz.mistake: Confuses the verb with the noun

quiz.q: 'Slow and steady wins the race' comes from which fable?
quiz.explain: In that fable, the steady tortoise beats the overconfident hare.
steps: 'Slow and steady wins the race' is the moral of a fable.
In 'The Hare and the Tortoise', the steady tortoise beats the hare.
So the answer is The Hare and the Tortoise.
Answer: The Hare and the Tortoise
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous fables

quiz.q: What is 'grit'?
options: courage and determination to keep going
quiz.explain: Grit means strong determination even when things are hard.
steps: 'Grit' here describes a quality of character.
It means courage and determination to keep going.
It is not a sweet, a shoe or a game.
Answer: courage and determination to keep going
quiz.mistake: Does not know this meaning of the word

teach.ask: Gappu sighs: 'I tried to build my nest three times and it fell. Should I just give up?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Perseverance means trying again and again. Nest number four, here I come!
teach.nudge: What's the big word for not giving up when things are hard?

revise.summary: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult or takes a long time. Its opposite is giving up, and many proverbs praise it.
focus: Meaning, synonyms and opposite of perseverance
remember: Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult or takes a long time.
Similar words: determination, persistence, grit. The opposite is giving up or quitting.
'Practice makes perfect', 'Slow and steady wins the race', 'Where there's a will, there's a way'.
'Rome was not built in a day' means big things take time.
traps: Perseverance is not luck or speed.
Don't confuse the verb 'determine' with the noun 'determination'.
'Slow and steady wins the race' comes from The Hare and the Tortoise, not another fable.

learn.hook: 'I CAN win', 'I MUST practise', 'I SHOULD rest' — little helping verbs carry big meanings!
points: Modal verbs are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb: can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would.
Can = ability ('I can run fast') or asking informally ('Can I go out?'). Could = past ability ('I could swim at six').
May = polite permission ('May I come in?') or possibility ('It may rain').
Must = something necessary or a strong duty ('You must wear a helmet'). Should = advice ('You should drink water').
After a modal, use the base verb with no 's', 'ed' or 'to': 'She can sing', not 'She can sings' or 'She can to sing'.

example.q: Think it through: Choose the best modal: 'Players ___ follow the rules of the game.' (can / must / may)
steps: Following rules is a duty, not just an ability or a possibility.
A strong duty is shown by 'must'.

learn.reallife: Rules and signs use modals: 'You must wear a seat belt', 'Visitors may take photos', 'You should wash your hands.'

items.text: You ___ wear a helmet while cycling.
You look tired. My advice: you ___ rest.
My clever little brother ___ already count to fifty.
When I was five, I ___ not swim.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the modal 'can' correctly?
quiz.explain: After a modal we use the base verb: can sing.
steps: After a modal, use the base verb with no -s and no 'to'.
can + sing = can sing.
So: She can sing beautifully.
Answer: She can sing beautifully.
quiz.mistake: Adds -s or 'to' after a modal

quiz.q: Which modal is used for polite permission?
quiz.explain: 'May I...?' is the polite way to ask permission.
steps: Polite permission is asked with 'May I...?'
'Must' shows a rule and 'should' gives advice.
So the modal is 'may'.
Answer: may
quiz.mistake: Uses 'must' to ask permission

quiz.q: 'You should eat more fruit.' Here 'should' shows:
quiz.explain: 'Should' gives advice or a suggestion.
steps: 'You should eat more fruit' is a suggestion.
'Should' is used to give advice.
It does not show ability or permission.
Answer: advice
quiz.mistake: Confuses advice with permission

quiz.q: Which modal shows a strict rule? 'All students ___ wear their ID cards in school.'
quiz.explain: A strict rule or duty uses 'must'.
steps: Wearing ID cards is a strict school rule.
A strict rule or duty uses 'must'.
Might, could and would are not for rules.
Answer: must
quiz.mistake: Does not see that this is a rule

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Look at those dark clouds. It ___ rain.'
quiz.explain: 'May' shows possibility; there is no 'to' after a modal.
steps: Dark clouds mean rain is possible.
'May' shows possibility, and no 'to' follows a modal.
So: It may rain.
Answer: may
quiz.mistake: Adds 'to' after a modal

quiz.q: 'I could ride a cycle when I was seven.' 'Could' here shows:
quiz.explain: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' for ability.
steps: 'Could' is the past form of 'can'.
'I could ride a cycle when I was seven' talks about past ability.
So it shows ability in the past.
Answer: ability in the past
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'could' shows advice

quiz.q: Which sentence shows ability?
options: Ravi can lift this heavy bag.
quiz.explain: 'Can' shows ability.
steps: 'Can' shows ability.
'Ravi can lift this heavy bag' tells what he is able to do.
Must (rule), should (advice) and may (permission) do not.
Answer: Ravi can lift this heavy bag.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ability with duty or advice

quiz.q: Fill in: 'To become a good runner, you ___ practise regularly.'
quiz.explain: 'Should' gives advice and is followed by the base verb without 'to'.
steps: Becoming a good runner needs practice: this is advice.
'Should' gives advice and takes the base verb with no 'to'.
So: you should practise regularly.
Answer: should
quiz.mistake: Adds 'to' or '-s' to a modal

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can, may, must, should — they all look like little helper words. What does each one do?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Can for ability, may for permission, must for duty and should for advice. I can fly and I must practise!
teach.nudge: Which modal would I use to give someone advice?

revise.summary: Modal verbs are helping verbs that add meaning to the main verb, such as ability, permission, possibility, duty or advice. After a modal, use the base verb.
focus: Choosing the right modal for ability, permission, possibility, duty or advice
Using the base verb after a modal
remember: Can = ability or informal asking; could = past ability.
May = polite permission ('May I come in?') or possibility ('It may rain').
Must = something necessary or a strong duty; should = advice.
After a modal, use the base verb with no 's', 'ed' or 'to': 'She can sing'.
traps: Don't add -s or 'to' after a modal: not 'can sings' or 'can to sing'.
Don't use 'must' to ask permission; use 'may'.
